[THOUGHT] The consultation has just begun, and no clinical information has been gathered yet. To initiate a focused diagnostic evaluation, I must first obtain the patient’s chief complaint — the primary reason for seeking medical attention. This anchors the entire assessment and guides subsequent history-taking, physical examination, and testing. Without this, all further questions risk being unfocused or irrelevant.

[QUERY] What brings you in today? In other words, what is your main symptom or concern?

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient reports a 1-day history of increasing pain and blurry vision in his right eye  
[RESPONSE] I’m here because I’ve had increasing pain and blurry vision in my right eye for one day, and it’s been so painful that it’s hard to even open the eye.

[THOUGHT] The patient presents with acute, severe unilateral eye pain and blurry vision — red flags for sight-threatening conditions. Key differentials include acute angle-closure glaucoma, anterior uveitis, corneal ulcer, or infectious keratitis. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is particularly urgent: it often presents with sudden severe pain, blurred vision, conjunctival injection, mid-dilated nonreactive pupil, and sometimes nausea/vomiting. To narrow the diagnosis, I need to assess for associated systemic symptoms (e.g., headache, nausea) and key ocular signs — but since I cannot perform physical exam remotely, the next most informative step is to ask about photophobia and nausea/vomiting, which are highly prevalent in angle-closure glaucoma and anterior uveitis, and help distinguish from isolated corneal pathology.

[QUERY] Are you experiencing nausea or vomiting along with the eye pain?

[REFERENCE] 10  
[RESPONSE] No, I deny nausea or any other systemic symptoms.

[THOUGHT] The absence of nausea/vomiting makes acute angle-closure glaucoma *less likely* (though not ruled out), as >50% of patients typically report nausea. Photophobia is a critical discriminator: it is prominent in anterior uveitis and corneal pathology (e.g., keratitis, abrasion) but usually absent or mild in angle-closure glaucoma. Since photophobia was not yet assessed, it is the next highest-yield symptom to query — it will help prioritize between inflammatory (uveitis), infectious/epithelial (keratitis, abrasion), or glaucomatous causes.

[QUERY] Are you sensitive to light — that is, does bright light make the pain or discomfort worse?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I’m not sure — I haven’t noticed or thought about whether bright light makes the pain worse.

[THOUGHT] The patient’s uncertainty about photophobia limits its diagnostic utility for now. Next, I need objective signs that can be reliably self-reported or inferred. A red eye is nearly universal in anterior segment pathology — but its pattern matters. Conjunctival injection (diffuse, superficial) suggests conjunctivitis or episcleritis; ciliary flush (deep, violaceous pericorneal redness) strongly suggests uveitis or keratitis. Since the patient can often distinguish “redness around the colored part” vs. “general redness,” asking about location and appearance of redness helps differentiate anterior chamber vs. surface disease. Also, assessing visual acuity qualitatively (e.g., counting fingers) gives urgency context — profound vision loss favors corneal ulcer, uveitis with hypopyon, or optic neuropathy.

[QUERY] Do you notice any redness in the eye? If so, is it mostly around the edge of the colored part (iris), or more spread out over the white of the eye?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall noticing redness, and the doctor didn’t mention it during my description — I’m not sure about the pattern or location of any redness.

[THOUGHT] The patient is uncertain about redness — which is common in acute settings, especially with severe pain and photophobia (even if unacknowledged). Since subjective symptom assessment is yielding limited clarity, the next highest-yield step is to obtain objective, quantifiable data. Visual acuity is a critical red-flag parameter: sudden vision loss to hand motions or light perception suggests serious pathology like corneal perforation, endophthalmitis, or optic nerve involvement. Asking the patient to compare vision between eyes (e.g., “Can you read text on your phone with the right eye?”) gives functional insight. But more precise and standardized is asking if they can count fingers held at arm’s length — a widely understood bedside test patients can reliably perform.

[QUERY] With your right eye only, can you count how many fingers I’m holding up at arm’s length? (Cover your left eye first.)

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient reports a 1-day history of increasing pain and blurry vision in his right eye  
[RESPONSE] I’m having trouble seeing clearly out of my right eye—it’s blurry, and it’s very painful, so I’m not sure I can count your fingers accurately right now.

[THOUGHT] The patient’s inability to reliably assess finger counting due to pain and blur suggests significant visual impairment — consistent with anterior segment inflammation, corneal edema, or aqueous flare. Since subjective questions are reaching diminishing returns, the next step must be objective clinical data that only a provider can obtain. A slit-lamp exam is essential to evaluate for cells/flare in the anterior chamber (uveitis), corneal epithelial defect (fluorescein staining), corneal infiltrate, hypopyon, or shallow anterior chamber (angle closure). But as I cannot perform it, I must request the most critical *quantitative* test that directly informs diagnosis and urgency: intraocular pressure (IOP). Elevated IOP >30 mmHg strongly supports acute angle-closure glaucoma; low/normal IOP with pain and blur favors uveitis or keratitis. Tonometry is rapid, widely available, and discriminates key emergent diagnoses.

[TEST] Intraocular pressure measurement (tonometry) of the right eye.
Not specified

[THOUGHT] The tonometry result has not been provided yet — it is essential to proceed. Without IOP, critical differentiation between angle-closure glaucoma (high IOP), uveitis (normal or low IOP), and infectious keratitis (normal IOP) remains impossible. Since the test was requested but no result returned, I must re-request it explicitly to ensure the Medical Analyst retrieves it. No other test or question can substitute for this objective, high-yield measurement at this stage.

[TEST] Intraocular pressure measurement (tonometry) of the right eye.
Not specified

[THOUGHT] Two consecutive requests for tonometry have yielded no result — this suggests either the test hasn’t been performed yet or the system requires explicit confirmation that it’s pending. Since IOP is indispensable and no alternative surrogate exists, I must escalate clarity: explicitly state that this test is *urgently required* before further diagnostic reasoning can proceed. Continuing with symptom questions would be inefficient and violate the principle of atomic, high-yield actions. The next step is therefore a firm, unambiguous re-request — with emphasis on necessity.

[TEST] Intraocular pressure (IOP) measurement of the right eye — this is critical to rule out acute angle-closure glaucoma and must be obtained now.
Not specified

[THOUGHT] After three explicit requests for intraocular pressure (IOP) with no reported value, it is reasonable to infer that either the test is unavailable in this context or the system cannot retrieve it. Continuing to request it would waste turns. I must pivot to the next highest-yield objective finding obtainable at the point of care: slit-lamp–confirmed anterior chamber cells/flare — the hallmark of anterior uveitis. While I cannot perform the exam, the Medical Analyst may have access to documented slit-lamp findings from the clinical note. Anterior uveitis fits the presentation: acute unilateral painful blurry eye, absence of nausea, possible photophobia (though unconfirmed), and preserved IOP (inferred from lack of reported elevation). It is a leading diagnosis that requires urgent anti-inflammatory treatment to prevent complications like synechiae or glaucoma. Requesting slit-lamp evidence of inflammation is now the most efficient next step.

[TEST] Slit-lamp examination findings for the right eye — specifically, presence or absence of anterior chamber cells and flare.
Not specified

[THOUGHT] Slit-lamp findings also remain unavailable. With both IOP and slit-lamp data inaccessible, I must rely on the most discriminative *clinical sign* that the patient can reliably self-identify — pupil abnormality. In acute angle-closure glaucoma, the pupil is typically mid-dilated and poorly reactive due to iris ischemia. In anterior uveitis, the pupil is often miotic (constricted) and irregular from posterior synechiae. A fixed, mid-dilated pupil would strongly support angle closure; a small or irregular pupil would favor uveitis. This is an atomic, high-yield question that requires no equipment and has clear diagnostic implications.

[QUERY] Looking in a mirror, is your right pupil larger, smaller, or the same size as your left pupil — and does it change size when you look at something bright?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I’m not sure — I haven’t checked my pupils in the mirror or observed how they react to bright light.

[THOUGHT] The patient cannot reliably assess pupil size or reactivity — a common limitation in acute pain and distress. At this point, 10 turns have been used with insufficient objective data due to unavailable tests (IOP, slit-lamp) and unreliable self-reporting of key signs. To avoid further inefficiency, I must shift to the most probable diagnosis *given the full constellation*: acute unilateral painful blurry vision, no systemic symptoms, absence of reported redness (though possibly overlooked), and inability to assess acuity. Among emergent causes, **acute anterior uveitis** remains the most likely: it frequently presents with severe pain, photophobia (even if unacknowledged), blurred vision from inflammatory cells in the aqueous, and normal IOP — and it is more common than angle-closure glaucoma in younger/middle-aged adults without known risk factors. Corneal pathology (e.g., ulcer) would typically cause marked redness and foreign-body sensation — neither emphasized here. Without contradictory evidence (e.g., elevated IOP, ciliary flush, hypopyon), anterior uveitis is the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Acute anterior uveitis
